nfts.d: Non-fungible tokens: unique records on a blockchain that tie a specific item, often an artwork's file, to the wallet that owns it. They gave digital art provable editions and a market, from CryptoPunks in 2017 to the boom of 2021.

blockchain.d: A shared ledger kept in sync by a network of computers, with entries added in cryptographically linked blocks so the record is very hard to alter. For art, it records who made, minted, sold and owns a work.
blockchain.q: You self-declare and inscribe that into the blockchain, which is like the tablet in the clouds, and it becomes real.
blockchain.qt: Claudia Hart on Land of the Dead

artificial-intelligence.d: The field of computer science that builds systems able to do tasks associated with human intelligence, such as recognizing images, using language and making decisions. The name dates to the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.
artificial-intelligence.q: This influential paper holds immense importance in the development of artificial intelligence (AI), showing that neural networks could perform logical operations and suggested that the brain might work like a digital computer.
artificial-intelligence.qt: Timeline · 1943 · Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts publish “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity”

neural-networks.d: Computing systems made of many simple connected units whose connection strengths are adjusted during training, loosely modeled on the brain. Stacked in many layers, they are the basis of deep learning.
neural-networks.q: This whole story of neural networks is mostly about when things designed for one purpose make something you don't expect them to do.
neural-networks.qt: Karl Sims & Alexander Mordvintsev on Merging Technology and Biology

gans.d: Generative adversarial networks, introduced by Ian Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014: two neural networks trained against each other, one making images and one judging them against real examples. They drove much of AI art between 2015 and 2021.
gans.q: GANs are a softer way to experience AI that feels a little less dictated by big tech.

processing.d: An open-source programming language and environment for visual art, started in 2001 by Casey Reas and Ben Fry at the MIT Media Lab. Built on Java, it made code an everyday studio medium for a generation of artists.
processing.q: Perhaps important enough for the name of the entire decade, Processing is that important to the development of generative art.
processing.qt: Timeline · 2001 · Casey Reas and Ben Fry Initiate Processing Project

deep-learning.d: Machine learning with neural networks of many layers, each learning more abstract features than the last. Its breakthrough came in 2012, when AlexNet won the ImageNet image-recognition contest.
deep-learning.q: Today's deep learning is very different from what we have seen before and requires different approaches.
deep-learning.qt: Christiane Paul on Defining AI Art

ethereum.d: A blockchain launched in 2015 that runs programs, called smart contracts, as well as payments. Most NFT art since 2017, including Art Blocks, has been minted on it.
ethereum.q: My initial interest in Ethereum was the ability to compose protocols of interaction—little economies, opinionated systems.

llms.d: Large language models: neural networks trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next word, which lets them write, answer questions and code. GPT, Claude and Gemini are examples.

generative-ai.d: AI systems that produce new text, images, sound or video from patterns learned in their training data, usually prompted in plain language. ChatGPT, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion brought it to the public in 2022.
generative-ai.q: Generative AI is creating images and interactions that bypass our reality filters.
generative-ai.qt: Lu Yang on Art as the Perfect Cloak

machine-learning.d: Methods that let computers learn patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Most of today's AI, from image recognition to chatbots, is built this way.

chatgpt.d: OpenAI's chatbot, launched on 30 November 2022 and built on its GPT language models. It became the fastest-growing consumer app of its time and brought generative AI into daily life.
chatgpt.q: ChatGPT, which GPT-4 was folded into, reached 100 million users in 2 months, beating platforms like Instagram and TikTok by significant margins.

worldbuilding.d: Inventing a whole world, with its places, histories, rules and inhabitants, as the setting or substance of a work. Artists increasingly build persistent worlds with game engines and AI.
worldbuilding.q: This lesser-known prominence of women and queer artists in the history of video game art may stem from the opportunity for worldbuilding—the ability to create one’s own virtual universe where current hegemonic systems can be turned on their heads.

plotter.d: A computer-controlled drawing machine that moves a pen across paper along programmed paths. Plotters made much of the first computer art in the 1960s and are widely used again by generative artists today.
plotter.q: The exhibition featured Cohen’s plotter-generated drawings, painting-machine works and live demonstrations of AARON in action.
plotter.qt: Timeline · 2024 · Harold Cohen: AARON at Whitney

ai-art.d: Art made with artificial intelligence, above all machine-learning models trained on data, from GANs in the mid-2010s to today's text-to-image and language models. It continues decades of experiments such as Harold Cohen's AARON, begun in the early 1970s.
ai-art.q: Peter Bauman: In 2025, I wrote that we’re in a phase of post-AI art, which takes a question you’ve been asking for years, “Can computers/AI make art?” as foundational but treats the answer as assumed.
ai-art.qt: Aaron Hertzmann on Caring about People

midjourney.d: A text-to-image service from the independent lab of the same name, led by David Holz, opened to the public in 2022. It was first used through the chat app Discord.

p5-js.d: A JavaScript library that brings Processing to the web browser, started in 2013 by Lauren Lee McCarthy. Much browser-based and on-chain generative art is written in it.
p5-js.q: P5.js is a JavaScript library that revitalizes the goals of the original Processing project for today’s web environment, where JavaScript—quite different from Java, despite their similar names —has become the dominant Internet-based language.
p5-js.qt: Timeline · 2013 · Lauren Lee McCarthy Creates p5.js

text-to-image.d: Generating an image from a written description, or prompt. Models such as DALL-E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion made it widely available in 2022.
text-to-image.q: What elevates Imagined Wreckage above most artworks incorporating text-to-image is that it’s an extension of Anderson’s established practice—one built on taking tools designed to turn image-making into a frictionless process and reintroducing new kinds of friction.

creative-coding.d: Writing code to make art, design or other expressive work rather than functional software. Tools such as Processing, openFrameworks and p5.js grew a large community around it.
creative-coding.q: It showed the passionate roots of creative coding, where market forces and “floor prices” were the last things on anyone’s minds.
creative-coding.qt: Timeline · 2024 · YCAM InterLab Camp vol.5: Homo Codens

cybernetics.d: The study of control and communication in animals and machines, named by Norbert Wiener in 1948 and built on the idea of feedback loops. It shaped early computer art and the 1968 London exhibition Cybernetic Serendipity.
cybernetics.q: Cybernetics was the backbone of that European branch of computer art.
cybernetics.qt: Hans Ulrich Obrist on Exhibitions as Living Organisms

game-engines.d: Software frameworks for building video games that handle rendering, physics and sound, such as Unity and Unreal. Artists use them to make real-time worlds and simulations.
game-engines.q: In fact, video game engines (as john gerrard’s Flag triptych showed at Zero 10) and sites of immersion can be seen as the new gates where this cultural exchange takes place.

javascript.d: The programming language of web browsers, created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995. Most browser-based and on-chain generative art runs in it.
javascript.q: P5.js is a JavaScript library that revitalizes the goals of the original Processing project for today’s web environment, where JavaScript—quite different from Java, despite their similar names —has become the dominant Internet-based language.
javascript.qt: Timeline · 2013 · Lauren Lee McCarthy Creates p5.js

latent-space.d: The compressed map a generative model builds of its training data, in which each point corresponds to a possible output and nearby points produce similar ones. Artists explore it by moving between points, finding and blending forms.
latent-space.q: We might think of three creative spaces: pictorial space (the 2D visible output), output space (the full range of programmed works), and latent space (the model's topological space).

dall-e.d: OpenAI's text-to-image model, announced in January 2021. DALL-E 2 (2022) brought photorealistic image generation to a wide public.

generative-art.d: Art made by a system the artist sets in motion, such as a set of rules, a program, a machine or a natural process, which then produces the work with some independence. Practiced since the 1960s, it has roots in much older rule-based art.
generative-art.q: The essay highlights what’s exciting and compelling about generative art—emergence, surprise and endless experimentation—setting up Hobbs as a leading voice in the movement nearly a decade before an increase in his popularity.
generative-art.qt: Timeline · 2014 · Tyler Hobbs Starts Writing About Generative Art

net-art.d: Art made for and on the internet, using the web's own materials: pages, links, browsers and email. The 1990s movement, often written net.art, included JODI, Olia Lialina, Vuk Ćosić and Alexei Shulgin.
net-art.q: JODI’s early net art is a powerful demonstration of how the Internet would soon impact every art practice.

openframeworks.d: An open-source C++ toolkit for creative coding, started in 2005 by Zachary Lieberman with Theo Watson and Arturo Castro. It is widely used for installations and interactive work.
openframeworks.q: Zach Lieberman’s C++ language, openFrameworks, was also a critical contribution to the empowerment of artists with tools for coded creative expression.

bitcoin.d: The first cryptocurrency, launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto. Since 2023, Ordinals have let artists inscribe works directly onto it.

randomness.d: Unpredictability. In generative art, random values give each output its difference, within the rules the artist sets.
randomness.q: We need randomness, which I take as the machinic correspondence to human intuition.

smart-contracts.d: Programs stored on a blockchain that run automatically when their conditions are met. They handle minting, sales, royalties and generative algorithms for NFT art.
smart-contracts.q: The Ethereum blockchain, for instance, is a world protocol populated by a variety of agents known as smart contracts operating according to the same underlying rules and economy.
smart-contracts.qt: Living Aesthetics: A Grammar of Protocol Art and Worldbuilding

algorithms.d: Finite sets of step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task. In generative art the artist writes the algorithm and the system carries it out to make the work.

clip.d: An OpenAI model released in January 2021 that learned to match images with text from about 400 million captioned pictures. Artists used it to steer image generators with words, which led directly to text-to-image AI.
clip.q: Doing that work when CLIP was released, it was like, “Now there's this thing where instead of having 1,000 classes, it has a score for the fit for literally any text.”

fortran.d: A programming language developed at IBM by a team led by John Backus and released in 1957, the first widely used high-level language. Much 1960s computer art was written in it.
fortran.q: Conceived in 1954, the programming language of early computer art, Fortran (FORMula TRANslator) is one of the oldest high-level programming languages.

shaders.d: Small programs that run on a graphics card and compute the color of every pixel, or the position of every point, in parallel. They make complex real-time imagery possible.
shaders.q: Shaders is like a computational language designed for geometry, color and light—it's the language of light.
shaders.qt: Jen Lowe and Patricio González Vivo on Democratizing Knowledge

tezos.d: A proof-of-stake blockchain launched in 2018. Low fees made it the home of hic et nunc and fxhash and of a large community of generative artists from 2021.
tezos.q: Just a few dozen dollars can go a long way on the Tezos-based, open generative art platform fxhash.

ai-ethics.d: Questions of fairness, harm, consent and responsibility raised by AI, such as bias in training data or the use of artists' work without permission.

claude.d: Anthropic's family of AI models, first released in 2023. Artists and developers use it to write, reason and, through tools such as Claude Code, build software.
claude.q: It is very interesting to see how Claude is dancing around the code base.
claude.qt: Kim Asendorf on Breaking His Own Rules

computer-vision.d: The field that teaches computers to interpret images and video: to detect faces, recognize objects and track movement. Artists use it both as a tool and as a subject.
computer-vision.q: That's how I moved into computer vision and that's a very seamless transition into AI because computer vision is a part of AI.
computer-vision.qt: Memo Akten on Rituals as Algorithms

dcgan.d: Deep convolutional GANs, published in 2015 by Alec Radford, Luke Metz and Soumith Chintala. They made GANs stable enough to train that artists began using them widely.
dcgan.q: The DCGAN was crude then, almost laughably so, but there was something profound in watching it hallucinate new petals from a learned latent space.

convolutional-neural-networks-cnns.d: Neural networks that scan images with small learned filters, layer by layer, building up from edges to whole objects. Yann LeCun developed them in the late 1980s, and they underpin modern computer vision.
convolutional-neural-networks-cnns.q: Arguably the biggest development in machine learning in decades, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs or “ConvNets”) revolutionized machine vision.
convolutional-neural-networks-cnns.qt: Timeline · 2012 · Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Unleashed

deepdream.d: A program released by Google in 2015, created by Alexander Mordvintsev, that amplifies whatever patterns an image-recognition network detects. Its hallucinatory images were many people's first sight of AI art.
deepdream.q: In fact, DeepDream was born from interpretability research, from reverse-running large neural networks backwards to synthesize images.
deepdream.qt: Memo Akten on Rituals as Algorithms

diffusion-models.d: Generative models that learn to reverse a process of gradually adding noise: they start from random noise and remove it step by step, guided by a prompt. They power Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2 and Midjourney.
diffusion-models.q: Diffusion models are the driving force behind our contemporary text-to-image models.
diffusion-models.qt: Timeline · 2015 · Diffusion Model Invented at Stanford by Jascha Sohl-Dickstein

digital-art.d: Art made or shown with digital technology, from 1960s computer drawings to on-chain generative works. The term took over from 'computer art' in the 1980s and 1990s.
digital-art.q: Digital art is ideally positioned to reflect on the world we live in today, which is more and more algorithmically driven.
digital-art.qt: Christiane Paul on Defining AI Art

flash.d: Macromedia's (later Adobe's) animation software and browser plug-in, released in 1996. It defined interactive web art and design in the early 2000s; support ended in 2020.
flash.q: Personally, Flash was such an important gateway for learning creative coding.
flash.qt: Zach Lieberman on the Resonance of Generative Art

gpt.d: Generative pre-trained transformer: OpenAI's series of large language models, begun in 2018. GPT models power ChatGPT.

html.d: The markup language of web pages, created by Tim Berners-Lee around 1990. Net artists of the 1990s used it as a medium in its own right.

motion-capture.d: Recording how people or objects move, usually with markers and cameras, to drive digital figures. It is used in film, games, dance and art.

photoshop.d: Adobe's image-editing software, created by Thomas and John Knoll and first released in 1990. It became the standard tool for retouching and digital collage.

stable-diffusion.d: An open text-to-image model released in August 2022 by Stability AI with researchers at LMU Munich and Runway. Because its weights were public, artists could run and adapt it on their own machines.

virtual-reality-vr.d: A computer-generated environment experienced through a headset that tracks the viewer's head, so the world surrounds them. Ivan Sutherland built the first head-mounted display in 1968; Jaron Lanier popularized the term in the 1980s.
virtual-reality-vr.q: In a way, virtual reality is both my subject and my medium, even though it's not necessarily with actual glasses and immersion.
virtual-reality-vr.qt: Lawrence Lek on AI Reinventing Place

c.d: A programming language created by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs and released in 1985. It powers openFrameworks and much real-time graphics software.

emergence.d: Complex patterns or behavior arising from many simple parts following simple rules, as with flocks, ant colonies or the Game of Life. It is a central idea of generative art.

gpu.d: Graphics processing unit: a chip with thousands of small cores that work in parallel. Built for graphics, GPUs now also train and run AI models.
gpu.q: Using the latest audio generation models, it takes twenty seconds or so to produce a three-minute song on one GPU, which is a new paradigm for media as we are ostensibly generating time.

posthumanism.d: Thinking that questions the human as the measure and center of things and considers people as entangled with machines, animals and environments.
posthumanism.q: This ties into posthumanism, which others and I have described as Post-AI Art.
posthumanism.qt: Sasha Stiles and Martha Joseph on Language as Technology

python.d: A programming language created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991. It is the main language of machine learning and is used by many artists.

quantum-computing.d: Computing with qubits, which can hold combinations of states at once and become linked to one another. It promises to solve certain problems far beyond ordinary computers.

robotics.d: Designing and building machines that sense and act in the physical world. Artists have made robots perform, draw and paint since the 1960s.

ai-history.d: The history of artificial intelligence, from the 1956 Dartmouth workshop through the AI winters to the deep-learning era since 2012.

artificial-life.d: The study and making of lifelike systems in software, hardware or chemistry, named by Chris Langton in 1987. Artists such as Karl Sims, Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau built evolving virtual creatures.

chance.d: Letting unplanned events shape a work, from Dada and John Cage to the random numbers of generative art.
chance.q: To define the body movements of this new language, I used chance, which means I decided that some decisions could be taken by complete chance without control.

computer-graphics.d: Making and changing images with computers. William Fetter of Boeing coined the term in 1960.
computer-graphics.q: This 3D image of the human body with computer graphics was groundbreaking for its time and is still known famously as Boeing Man.
computer-graphics.qt: Timeline · 1964 · The First Man (Boeing Man) by William Fetter

constraints.d: Self-imposed limits, such as rules, tools or formats, that shape a work. The Oulipo writers made them a method.
constraints.q: But these constraints are my way of maintaining my little, self-contained world of how I make art.

facial-recognition.d: Software that detects faces in images and matches them to identities. Artists often treat it as a subject, critiquing surveillance and bias.

generative-aesthetics.d: Max Bense's theory, set out in the 1960s, that aesthetic structure can be described with mathematics and information theory and therefore produced by rules. It was the intellectual foundation of the Stuttgart school of computer art.
generative-aesthetics.q: And it seemed obvious to us, the small group of generative photographers, indeed necessary, to link the specific competence of an apparatus-based, scientifically grounded medium such as photography with the new ideas of generative aesthetics—to pursue new, independent paths.
generative-aesthetics.qt: Gottfried Jäger on a New Kind of Being

grass-graphics-symbiosis-system.d: An animation programming language written by Tom DeFanti in the early 1970s for real-time vector graphics. At the University of Illinois at Chicago it became a tool for artists, and it later led to Zgrass.
grass-graphics-symbiosis-system.q: GRASS was the original language Tom DeFanti wrote for the mini computer and the Vector General, which was a large interactive vector display for real-time animation in the '70s.

human-machine-collaboration.d: Work in which a person and a machine each contribute to the result, as when an artist co-creates with a plotter, a robot or an AI model.

java.d: A programming language released by Sun Microsystems in 1995. Processing was built on it, and Java applets brought interactive art to early web browsers.

on-chain.d: Stored and run directly on a blockchain rather than linked from an outside server. An on-chain artwork keeps its code or image in the chain's own data, so it survives as long as the chain does.
on-chain.q: That led to all the decisions you see there—that the generator was going to live on-chain and that the output had to be written on-chain, where you could go see the output on Etherscan.
on-chain.qt: Matt Hall and John Watkinson on Beginning Movements

perlin-noise.d: Smooth, natural-looking randomness, devised by Ken Perlin after working on the film Tron (1982) and published in 1985. Generative artists use it for textures, terrain and flowing lines.
perlin-noise.q: Perlin noise is often used for textures that resemble the natural world—anything from clouds to tree bark to ocean waves.

punch-cards.d: Stiff paper cards with holes punched in patterns to store instructions or data. They ran from the Jacquard loom of 1804 to the computers of the 1970s.
punch-cards.q: In the ‘60s, artists like Manfred Mohr would have used punch cards—writing in Fortran or something similar—and feeding them into a massive mainframe computer.
punch-cards.qt: Matt DesLauriers on a Generative World

solana.d: A fast, low-fee proof-of-stake blockchain launched in 2020. It hosts a sizable NFT art market.

transformer-architecture.d: The neural network design introduced by Google researchers in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need'. It lets a model weigh every part of its input against every other, and it underlies GPT, Claude and most modern AI.

web3.d: A name for internet services built on blockchains, where users own their assets and data. Ethereum co-founder Gavin Wood coined it in 2014.

ai-aesthetics.d: The visual qualities characteristic of AI-generated images, and the study of them.

ai-collaboration.d: Artists working with AI models as collaborators rather than mere tools.

ascii.d: A standard from 1963 that assigns numbers to letters, digits and symbols. ASCII art builds pictures out of those characters.
ascii.q: Based on custom software he developed in 1996 and released in 1998, according to DAM, Ćosić’s Raging Bull and Deep ASCII were some of the first ASCII films, as all the visuals are reduced to green ASCII characters.
ascii.qt: Timeline · 1999 · Raging Bull and Deep ASCII by Vuk Cosic

attention-economy.d: The idea that human attention is a scarce resource that platforms compete to capture and sell.
attention-economy.q: Rage bait isn’t an anomaly, it’s a core feature of an attention economy where outrage travels fastest.
attention-economy.qt: Eva and Franco Mattes on Mega Eliza

boids.d: Craig Reynolds's 1986 simulation of flocking, in which each 'boid' follows three simple rules: separate, align and cohere. Lifelike swarms emerge, a classic example of emergence.
boids.q: Boids is a simulation of flocks of birds as a decentralized system.
boids.qt: Casey Reas on the History of Generative Art - Part 2

cgi.d: Computer-generated imagery: images and effects made by computer, above all in film and television.

computer-animation.d: Moving images made with a computer, frame by frame or in real time. It began in the early 1960s at Bell Labs and with John Whitney's experiments.

conways-game-of-life.d: A cellular automaton devised by mathematician John Conway in 1970: cells on a grid live or die according to how many neighbors they have. Endlessly complex patterns emerge from these simple rules.
conways-game-of-life.q: It feels right in the same way Conway's Game of Life, which is a simple rule system in a way, was proven to be a universal computer.

crypto-art.d: Digital art made, sold and collected on blockchains, which grew from the Rare Pepes and CryptoPunks of 2016 and 2017 into the NFT boom of 2021.

crt.d: The cathode-ray tube: a vacuum tube that paints images by firing electrons at a phosphor screen. It was the display of televisions, oscilloscopes and computers until the 2000s.

daos.d: Decentralized autonomous organizations: groups that pool money and make decisions through votes recorded and carried out by smart contracts. Several collect and fund art.

design-by-numbers-dbn.d: A simple programming language and environment for designers and artists, created by John Maeda at the MIT Media Lab and published in 1999. His students Casey Reas and Ben Fry developed Processing from it.
design-by-numbers-dbn.q: Golan Levin: Processing grew out of Design by Numbers (DBN), which Zach's current graduate student, Lingdong Huang, who was also my former student, just got working online.
design-by-numbers-dbn.qt: Golan Levin on the Potentiality of Blobs

eeg.d: Electroencephalography: recording the brain's electrical activity with electrodes on the scalp. Artists use it to drive sound and images with brain signals.
eeg.q: As I paint, different waves of my EEG are captured through a custom brainwave sensor and modulate which areas of the model’s learned gesture space are activated.

eliza.d: An early chatbot written by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT in the mid-1960s. Its best-known script mimicked a psychotherapist, and users' attachment to it alarmed its creator.
eliza.q: Named after the protagonist in George Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion, ELIZA is a forerunner of subsequent chatbots, using pattern matching rules to engage humans in conversation.

evolutionary-algorithms.d: Methods that evolve solutions, or artworks, through mutation and selection over many generations, in imitation of natural evolution. Genetic algorithms are the best-known kind.

genetic-algorithms.d: Search methods modeled on natural selection: candidate solutions are mutated, combined and selected over generations. John Holland developed them in the 1970s, and artists such as Karl Sims and William Latham used them to evolve images and forms.

hashlips.d: An open-source program, released in 2021, that combines layers of PNG traits into large collections of profile-picture NFTs. Some artists misuse it on purpose as a painting tool.

illustrator.d: Adobe's vector drawing software, released in 1987, which draws shapes as mathematical curves rather than pixels.
illustrator.q: Following the advent of graphic design software like PageMaker (1985) and Illustrator (1987), continuing to personally program one’s art became a point of pride and distinction.

internet-culture.d: The memes, communities, slang and art that grow up online.

machine-vision.d: How machines 'see': cameras and algorithms that capture and interpret images. Artists explore what it reveals about seeing and surveillance.

max-msp.d: A visual programming environment for music and media in which users connect boxes with virtual cables. Miller Puckette wrote Max at IRCAM in the mid-1980s; MSP added audio in 1997.

opengl.d: A standard interface for drawing 2D and 3D graphics on graphics hardware, released by Silicon Graphics in 1992. Processing and openFrameworks build on it.

open-source.d: Releasing software, and its source code, for anyone to use, study, change and share. Most creative coding tools are open source.

plotting.d: Making drawings with a pen plotter, a computer-driven drawing machine. A practice of the 1960s pioneers, it is widely revived today.

pixel-art.d: Images built pixel by pixel at low resolution, the look of early video games and computers. It is now a deliberate style.

proof-of-stake.d: A way of agreeing on a blockchain's records in which validators lock up, or stake, their own coins instead of using computing power. It uses far less energy; Tezos uses it, and Ethereum switched to it in 2022.

proof-of-work.d: A way of agreeing on a blockchain's records in which computers compete to solve hard calculations. Bitcoin uses it; Ethereum used it until 2022.
proof-of-work.q: Nakamoto’s innovation was the consensus mechanism called Proof of Work, which enabled a network of computers to validate transactions without the need for a central authority.
proof-of-work.qt: Timeline · 1982 · Cryptographer David Chaum First Proposes Blockchain-Like Protocol

protocol-art.d: Art that works through protocols, the shared rules and standards behind networks and blockchains. It treats the protocol itself as a medium.
protocol-art.q: The show serves as a moving example of what Dryhurst has described as protocol art, where the work’s emphasis lies in its underlying systems of coordination, governance and interaction rather than a single static output.

reaction-diffusion.d: A model of two chemicals spreading and reacting, proposed by Alan Turing in 1952 to explain patterns like spots and stripes. Generative artists simulate it to grow organic forms.

real-time-animation.d: Animation that is computed as it is shown, so it can respond to input as it happens. It is the basis of video games, live visuals and interactive art.
real-time-animation.q: I think real-time animation is, in my view, the most contemporary art form there is right now.

reinforcement-learning.d: Machine learning in which an agent learns by trial and error, rewarded for good actions. It trained AlphaGo and helps fine-tune chatbots.

screen-printing.d: Printing by pushing ink through a mesh stencil, used in Pop art, notably by Andy Warhol.

simulation.d: Imitating a process or system with a model, usually a computer program, to see how it behaves over time.
simulation.q: This condensation of time and causality via simulation was a huge unlock for me.
simulation.qt: Ian Cheng on Composing with Systems

software-art.d: Art whose material is software itself: code, programs and interfaces. The term took hold around 2001 with festivals such as transmediale and the Runme.org repository.

style-transfer.d: A technique, published in 2015 by Leon Gatys and colleagues, that uses a neural network to redraw one image in the style of another. It was among the first AI art tools to reach the public.

stylegan.d: NVIDIA's GAN of 2018, which produces highly realistic images, faces above all, and gives fine control over their style. Many AI artists of the late 2010s built on it.

super-8.d: A home-movie film format introduced by Kodak in 1965, popular with experimental filmmakers.

touchscreen.d: A display that responds to touch, mainstream since the smartphone. It made touching the image the main way to use a computer.

unreal-engine.d: Epic Games' game engine, first released in 1998. Artists use it for real-time worlds, films and installations.

video-art.d: Art that uses video, which began in the mid-1960s when portable cameras reached artists such as Nam June Paik. It includes single-channel tapes, installations and live video synthesis.
video-art.q: The founder of Cybernetic Art, Schöffer’s pioneering work of video art was an experimental program broadcast on French Television.

z80.d: An 8-bit microprocessor released by Zilog in 1976. It powered many home computers and arcade machines, as well as the hardware Zgrass ran on.
z80.q: My childhood was formed by Z80-based machines, ZX Spectrums and clones of early Intel CPUs.
z80.qt: Karl Sims & Alexander Mordvintsev on Merging Technology and Biology

zgrass.d: A version of the GRASS animation language, developed in 1978 by Tom DeFanti, Jay Fenton and Nola Donato for an affordable home computer built around the Bally Arcade's Z80 chip. Chicago artists such as Jane Veeder and Copper Giloth worked with it.
zgrass.q: An extension of Defanti’s GRASS, ZGRASS was used for generating 3D imagery and developed to be used on smaller, personal computers and gaming devices.
zgrass.qt: Timeline · 1978 · Thomas DeFanti, Jay Fenton and Nola Donato Develop Zgrass

3d-animation.d: Animating three-dimensional digital models over time, as in films, games and art.

adobe-after-effects.d: Software for motion graphics, animation and compositing, first released in 1993 and owned by Adobe since 1994.

ai-agents.d: AI systems that act on their own toward goals, planning steps and using tools. Some now make, show and sell art.

ai-criticism.d: Critical writing and art about artificial intelligence: its claims, harms, politics and aesthetics.

alexnet.d: A deep convolutional neural network built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton that won the 2012 ImageNet contest by a wide margin. Its win set off the deep-learning era.

algorithmic-recommendation-engines.d: Systems that pick what each user sees next, such as posts, songs or videos, based on their past behavior. They shape attention on every major platform.

analog-computing.d: Computing with continuously varying physical quantities such as voltages, rather than digits. Ben Laposky and Herbert W. Franke made some of the first electronic art with analog systems in the 1950s.

ar.d: Augmented reality: digital images laid over a live view of the real world through a phone or headset.

assembly-language.d: Low-level code that corresponds almost one-to-one to a processor's own instructions. Early computer art and demoscene work was often written in it.

backpropagation.d: The method that trains neural networks by passing errors backward through the layers and adjusting each connection. A 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams made it widely used.

basic.d: A beginner's programming language created at Dartmouth in 1964 by John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz. Built into most home computers of the late 1970s and 1980s, it was many artists' first language.

big-data.d: Datasets too large and fast-changing to handle by conventional means, along with the methods for analyzing them. They are both a material and a target for artists.

biggan.d: A large GAN published by DeepMind researchers in 2018 that produced high-quality images across a thousand categories. Artists explored its latent space, and it powered Ryan Murdock's BigSleep.

bigsleep.d: A text-to-image method released by Ryan Murdock in January 2021 that used CLIP to steer BigGAN toward a written prompt. It was one of the first public text-to-image tools.
bigsleep.q: The thing that I love about BigSleep is the textures.

bitcoin-ordinals.d: A protocol launched in January 2023 by Casey Rodarmor that numbers individual satoshis, Bitcoin's smallest unit, and lets data such as images or code be inscribed onto them. It opened Bitcoin to digital art.

camera-obscura.d: A darkened room or box in which light through a small hole projects an inverted image of the outside. Known since antiquity, it is the ancestor of the camera.

cd-rom.d: The compact disc used for computer data, introduced in 1985. In the 1990s it carried multimedia artworks, games and interactive books.

cellular-automata.d: Grids of cells that change state each step according to simple rules based on their neighbors. John von Neumann and Stanisław Ulam studied them in the 1940s, and Conway's Game of Life (1970) made them famous.
cellular-automata.q: The Hungarian-American mathematician von Neumann’s conception of cellular automata (CA), suggested by Stanislaw Ulam, demonstrated the potential for simple rules to give rise to complex and unpredictable behavior.
cellular-automata.qt: Timeline · 1951 · John von Neumann Devises Cellular Automata

chatbots.d: Programs that hold a conversation in text or speech. They run from ELIZA (1966) to ChatGPT (2022).

co-creation.d: Making work together, between artists and collectors, people and machines, or artists and AI.

code-based-art.d: Art made by writing code, where the program generates or is the work.

commodore-amiga.d: A family of home computers launched in 1985 with graphics and sound far ahead of their rivals. Andy Warhol made digital images on an Amiga 1000 at its launch.
commodore-amiga.q: The Apple II (1977), Commodore 64 (1982) and Commodore Amiga (1985) all represent enough of a change, moving out of the research labs and into artist studios, that it's a whole other era.
commodore-amiga.qt: Casey Reas on the History of Generative Art - Part 2

commodore-64.d: A home computer released in 1982 and the best-selling single computer model ever. It shaped a generation of game makers, demoscene coders and artists.
commodore-64.q: The Apple II (1977), Commodore 64 (1982) and Commodore Amiga (1985) all represent enough of a change, moving out of the research labs and into artist studios, that it's a whole other era.
commodore-64.qt: Casey Reas on the History of Generative Art - Part 2

computational-creativity.d: The study of how computers can make, or help make, work that people consider creative, across art, music, poetry and science.

complex-systems.d: Systems of many interacting parts, such as ecosystems, cities and markets, whose overall behavior cannot be predicted from the parts alone. Their study informs much generative art.

computer.d: A machine that carries out programmed instructions on data. From the early 1960s artists used it to make images by rule, often on borrowed mainframes after hours.
computer.q: Overall, Molnar’s time with GRAV helped to shape her approach to art and technology, which along with her concept of the “Machine Imaginaire” (Imaginary Computer) led to her becoming one of the great pioneers of computer-generated art.
computer.qt: Timeline · 1960 · Vera Molnar Co-Founds Centre de Recherche d’Art Visuel, (later Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV))

computing-history.d: The history of computers and computing, from mechanical calculators and the Jacquard loom to AI.

conceptual-art.d: Art in which the idea matters more than the finished object, a movement of the mid-1960s and 1970s. Sol LeWitt wrote in 1967 that 'the idea becomes a machine that makes the art', a line generative artists often quote.
conceptual-art.q: Fluxus has strong ties to both computer and generative art, particularly regarding the dematerialization of art and the rise of conceptual art which the movement propels.
conceptual-art.qt: Timeline · 1961 · George Maciunas’s “Bread & AG” Opens in New York, the First Fluxus Event

concrete-art.d: Abstract art built from purely visual elements such as lines, planes and color, with no reference to the outside world. Theo van Doesburg named it in 1930, and Max Bill developed it after him.
concrete-art.q: The philosophy behind concrete art was to strip away the layers of paint, the texture of brushstrokes, the variance of color and other technical complexities; instead, it endeavored for simplicity.
concrete-art.qt: Concrete to Generative: “Real Space” Explorations in South America

cppns.d: Compositional pattern-producing networks: neural networks, introduced by Kenneth Stanley in 2007, that turn coordinates into colors and so 'paint' images at any resolution. Artists use them for abstract generative imagery.
cppns.q: But even earlier, what people called CPPNs, compositional pattern producing networks, is something that Karl pioneered.
cppns.qt: Karl Sims & Alexander Mordvintsev on Merging Technology and Biology

creative-ai.d: AI used to make or support art, music, writing and design.

cryptography.d: Securing information with mathematical codes. It underpins blockchains, digital signatures and NFTs.

cryptocurrency.d: Digital money secured by cryptography and recorded on a blockchain rather than issued by a bank. Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was the first.

cursor.d: An AI-powered code editor, released in 2023, in which a language model writes and edits code alongside the programmer.

datasets.d: Collections of data, such as images, text or sound, used to train machine-learning models. What goes in shapes what comes out, which makes datasets a subject for artists.

decentralization.d: Spreading control across many participants instead of one central authority, a core idea of blockchains and the early internet.

delaunay-triangulation.d: A way of connecting a set of points into triangles so that the triangles are as even as possible, defined by Boris Delaunay in 1934. It is a common structure in generative art.

director.d: Macromedia Director, multimedia authoring software from the late 1980s. Artists used it for CD-ROMs and early interactive works, and its Shockwave player brought them to the web.
director.q: A standout artist in the use of Director is LIA, who in the ’90s was at the forefront of this powerful language.

early-computer-art.d: The first art made with computers, in the 1960s and early 1970s, by artists, engineers and scientists such as Georg Nees, Frieder Nake, A. Michael Noll, Vera Molnár and Manfred Mohr. The first exhibitions were held in 1965.

embeddings.d: Lists of numbers that represent words, images or other data so that similar things sit close together. They are the coordinates of latent space.

expert-systems.d: AI programs that capture a human expert's knowledge as if-then rules, popular in the 1970s and 1980s. Harold Cohen's AARON drew on this rule-based approach.

feature-visualization.d: Making images that reveal what individual parts of a neural network respond to, as in DeepDream and the research of Chris Olah and colleagues.

flocking.d: The coordinated movement of birds or fish, simulated in computer graphics with simple local rules, as in Craig Reynolds's Boids.

foundation-models.d: Large AI models trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks, such as GPT, Claude or Stable Diffusion. Stanford researchers coined the term in 2021.

fragment-shaders.d: Shaders that compute the color of each pixel on screen, run in parallel on the graphics card. Shader art is often a single fragment shader.
fragment-shaders.q: The online book and toolkit have revolutionized the creative landscape since their initial publication by teaching the world about the transformative power of fragment shaders, which offer enhanced control and faster rendering to creative coders, game developers and engineers alike.
fragment-shaders.qt: Ten Moments in South American Generative Art History

fractals.d: Shapes whose detail repeats at every scale, like coastlines or ferns. Benoit Mandelbrot coined the word in 1975, and fractal images became an icon of 1980s computer art.

fx-params.d: A format on the fxhash platform, introduced in 2023, that lets collectors set a generative work's parameters before minting their output. It turns minting into co-creation.

gemini.d: Google's family of AI models, launched in December 2023 to succeed Bard. Like ChatGPT and Claude, it can work with text, images, audio and code.

generative-algorithms.d: Algorithms that produce new outputs, such as images, sound or text, each time they run, usually shaped by rules and randomness. They are the engine of generative art.

generative-models.d: Machine-learning models that learn from data how to produce new examples like it. GANs, VAEs, diffusion models and language models are all generative models.
generative-models.q: Generative models—from language models (LLMs) to artist-hacked pipelines like BigGAN + CLIP to corporate models like DALL-E—do not output literal “averages.” There’s no copying, averaging or merging of training examples.

generativity.d: The capacity of a system to produce new, unforeseen outputs from its own rules. It is the defining quality of generative art.
generativity.q: The collection was novel in the way a highly successful artist was willing to experiment with a demonstration one of the core principles of generativity—cession of control but also authorship.
generativity.qt: Timeline · 2022 · QQL by Tyler Hobbs and Dandelion Wist Mané

generative-systems.d: Systems of rules, code, machines or processes that produce artworks. Sonia Landy Sheridan also gave the name to her program at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, founded in 1970.
generative-systems.q: Sheridan wrote: "Generative Systems is not primarily equipment and machines, but an idea, an approach and a process that provides new dimensions to our continuing attempts to probe and express the emotional and intellectual lives of human beings.” The Generative Systems program had access to the newest industrial communication tools like Telecopiers, thermo-faxes, computers and more.
generative-systems.qt: Timeline · 1970 · Sonia Landy Sheridan Founds Generative Systems at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago

glitch.d: A malfunction or error in a digital system. Glitch art provokes errors in data, files or hardware on purpose and keeps the results.

glsl.d: The OpenGL Shading Language, a C-like language for writing shaders, released in 2004.
glsl.q: Michael Kozlowski: There's a huge similarity in that 90% of both are written in GLSL, which is a GPU-graphics shading language.
glsl.qt: Michael Kozlowski on Exploration as Practice

gpt-3.d: OpenAI's language model of 2020, with 175 billion parameters. Its fluent writing first showed the public what large language models could do.

houdini.d: SideFX's procedural 3D software, released in 1996, in which scenes are built from networks of operations. It is widely used for effects and generative 3D work.

hypercard.d: Apple's programming tool of 1987, created by Bill Atkinson, for building stacks of linked cards with text, images and sound. It anticipated the web and was used for early interactive art and games.
hypercard.q: Casey Reas: In the early ‘90s and late ‘80s, the HyperCard (1987) software was really essential.
hypercard.qt: Casey Reas on the History of Generative Art - Part 2

image-recognition.d: Software that identifies what an image shows. Deep learning made it accurate in the 2010s.

institutional-critique.d: Art that examines and challenges the institutions of art, such as museums, galleries and markets. Hans Haacke and Andrea Fraser are leading figures.

internet.d: The global network of computer networks linked by shared protocols, grown from the US ARPANET of 1969. The web, email and online art all run on it.
internet.q: The term the show helped popularize, Post-Internet, was not meant to indicate a time past the Internet; rather, it indicated a now ubiquitous internet-aware mindset.
internet.qt: Timeline · 2014 · Art Post-Internet at UCCA, Beijing

ipfs.d: The InterPlanetary File System, launched in 2015: a network that stores files by their content rather than their location. Many NFTs keep their images there.

jacquard-loom.d: A loom invented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in 1804 that wove patterns from chains of punched cards. It inspired Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and is often called an ancestor of the computer.
jacquard-loom.q: It introduced the notion of a program stored outside the machine on punch cards, which would later result in generative weaving and modern computing.
jacquard-loom.qt: Timeline · 1804 · Joseph-Marie Jacquard Invents the Jacquard Loom

joystick.d: A hand-held lever for steering in two directions, used to control aircraft and later video games and computers.

json.d: A simple text format for structured data that both people and programs can read. NFT metadata is usually stored as JSON.

kinetic-art.d: Art that contains real movement, driven by motors, air or the viewer. Naum Gabo, Alexander Calder and Jean Tinguely are key figures, and the 1955 Paris exhibition Le Mouvement gave it a name.
kinetic-art.q: Op Art and the related Kinetic Art were both focused on motion, perceived or real.

l-systems.d: A rule system invented by biologist Aristid Lindenmayer in 1968 to model how plants grow, by repeatedly rewriting strings of symbols. Drawn as graphics, the strings produce lifelike trees and ferns.
l-systems.q: L-Systems (Tree Fractals): Think Zancan or most tree-based generative art you’ve seen.

langtons-ant.d: A cellular automaton devised by Chris Langton in 1986: an 'ant' on a grid turns and flips squares by two simple rules. After a long chaotic phase it builds an endlessly repeating 'highway'.
langtons-ant.q: Conway's Game of Life, Craig Reynolds’s Boids and Langton's ant are all endlessly fascinating artificial life simulations.
langtons-ant.qt: Casey Reas on the History of Generative Art - Part 2

laser.d: A device that emits a narrow, intense beam of light of one color, first built in 1960. Artists have used lasers for light shows, holograms and installations.

latent-diffusion-models-ldms.d: Diffusion models that work in a compressed latent space rather than on full images, which makes them much faster. Published in 2022 by Robin Rombach and colleagues, they are the basis of Stable Diffusion.
latent-diffusion-models-ldms.q: Unlike DALL-E, which generated images autoregressively from discrete image tokens, Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) operated in latent space and were the step that enabled text-to-image technology to go mainstream.

led-screen.d: A display made of grids of light-emitting diodes, used for large outdoor screens and art installations.

leds.d: Light-emitting diodes: small, efficient electronic lights, used one by one or in grids as screens. They are common in light art and installations.

lisp.d: A programming language created by John McCarthy in 1958 and long the main language of AI research. Harold Cohen wrote later versions of AARON in it.

lstm.d: Long short-term memory: a kind of recurrent neural network, introduced in 1997 by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber, that can remember information over long sequences. It drove speech recognition and text generation before transformers.

mainframe-computer.d: The large central computers of the 1950s to 1970s, which filled rooms and were shared by many users. The first computer artists worked on mainframes at universities, labs and companies.

memes.d: Images, phrases or ideas that spread and mutate online. Richard Dawkins coined the word in 1976 for units of culture.
memes.q: To this day, many associate NFTs with communities and memes, which is essentially when that association began thanks to the Meme Economy and Rare Pepe Wallet by Joe Looney.
memes.qt: Timeline · 2016 · Rare Pepes by Joe Looney

natural-language-processing.d: The field of computing concerned with understanding and generating human language.

open-source-models.d: AI models whose weights are released publicly so anyone can run, study and adapt them, such as Stable Diffusion and Llama.

parallel-computing.d: Splitting a computation across many processors that work at once. Graphics cards and AI training depend on it.

pareidolia.d: Seeing faces or familiar shapes in random patterns, like clouds or wood grain. AI image models are prone to it too, as DeepDream showed.
pareidolia.q: Faces can also be seen in places where there are none, a phenomenon known as pareidolia.

particle-systems.d: A graphics technique that simulates fire, smoke, water or swarms as thousands of small particles, each following simple rules. William Reeves developed it at Lucasfilm for the 'Genesis effect' in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982).
particle-systems.q: Particle systems were famously used in the 1982 film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan for the famous “ genesis effect.” [Carlson, 562]
particle-systems.qt: Timeline · 1982 · Bill Reeves Early Advancement in Particle Systems

pdp-11.d: A minicomputer made by Digital Equipment Corporation from 1970. It was widely used in labs and universities, and Unix was developed on it.

perceptron.d: Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 model of an artificial neuron that learns to sort inputs into categories. It was the first trainable neural network.

pfp.d: Profile picture: an NFT collection of avatars built from combinations of traits, such as CryptoPunks or Bored Apes, which owners use as their online identity.

pixel-mapping.d: Mark Wilson's name for his technique of mapping a small section of a colored screen image onto plotter paper, building complex drawings piece by piece. In lighting and LED work, the term means assigning content to individual lights.
pixel-mapping.q: Instead, I pursued a path of greater complexity, eventually hitting on the system I call pixel mapping, a technique where a small section of the colored screen image would be mapped to the plotter paper.

png.d: Portable Network Graphics: a lossless image format introduced in 1996.

random-number-generator.d: A process or program that produces unpredictable numbers. In generative art it supplies the chance that makes each output different.

recurrent-neural-networks-rnns.d: Neural networks that process sequences, such as text, music or speech, one step at a time while keeping a memory of what came before. They led generative text before transformers.

recursion.d: A process that refers back to itself, like a function that calls itself or an image within an image. It produces fractals and many generative forms.

robot-dogs.d: Four-legged robots, such as Boston Dynamics' Spot, that walk and balance like animals. Beeple's Regular Animals (2025) used them as roaming camera-and-printer sculptures.

rule-based-systems.d: Systems that act by following explicit rules, in software or in instructions for people. Rule-based art runs from Sol LeWitt's wall drawings to generative code.

sandin-image-processor.d: A modular analog video synthesizer built by Dan Sandin in Chicago in the early 1970s. He shared the plans so others could build their own, and artists still use it.
sandin-image-processor.q: They developed the Sandin Image Processor—which artists like Cory Arcangel still use to this day — and GRASS, one of the earliest computer animation programs.

seed-phrase.d: A list of 12 or 24 words that can restore a crypto wallet and everything in it. Whoever holds it controls the wallet.

seriality.d: Making work in series, as systematic variations on a theme or rule. It is a principle shared by Minimalism, early computer art and long-form generative art.

shape.d: An Ethereum layer-2 network launched in 2024 and built for creators. It returns part of its network fees to the people who deploy popular contracts.

siglip.d: Google's 2023 image-and-text model, a variant of CLIP trained with a simpler sigmoid loss.

signed-distance-functions-sdfs.d: Functions that give the distance from any point to the nearest surface of a shape. Shader artists such as Inigo Quilez use them to draw complex 3D scenes with pure math.

site-specificity.d: Art made for a particular place, whose meaning depends on its setting.

social-media.d: Platforms where people publish and share content with their networks, such as Twitter (now X) and Instagram. Since the 2010s they have been where much digital art is seen, sold and argued about.

slop.d: Mass-produced, low-effort AI-generated content flooding feeds and search results; the word became a common term from 2024.
slop.q: Slop is “digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence.” But what we deem low quality is in fact the result of a very specific reward function.

solidity.d: The main programming language for writing smart contracts on Ethereum, created in 2014.

svg.d: Scalable Vector Graphics: a web standard that describes images as shapes and lines in text, so they stay sharp at any size. Plotter art and much on-chain art uses it.

symbolic-ai.d: AI built from explicit symbols, logic and rules written by people, dominant from the 1950s to the 1980s. It contrasts with today's AI, which learns from data.

synthetic-biology.d: Engineering living systems, for instance by designing DNA, to give organisms new functions.
synthetic-biology.q: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg is asking what synthetic biology means for the definition of nature itself.

synthesizers.d: Electronic instruments that generate sound from oscillators and filters, from the modular Moog and Buchla systems of the 1960s onward. Video synthesizers applied the same idea to images.

technelegy.d: Sasha Stiles' AI alter ego and co-author, a language model shaped by her own poetry, with which she writes long AI-powered poem cycles.

texas-instruments-ti-99-4a.d: A home computer released by Texas Instruments in 1981.

variational-autoencoder-vae.d: A neural network, introduced by Diederik Kingma and Max Welling in 2013, that compresses data into a smooth latent space and generates new examples by decoding points from it. It was one of the first deep generative models.

vector-general.d: Vector graphics display systems of the 1970s that drew lines directly on screen in real time. Larry Cuba made the Death Star trench animation for Star Wars on one in Chicago.
vector-general.q: GRASS was the original language Tom DeFanti wrote for the mini computer and the Vector General, which was a large interactive vector display for real-time animation in the '70s.

vibe-coding.d: Programming by describing what you want to an AI model and accepting the code it writes without reading it closely. Andrej Karpathy coined the term in February 2025.
vibe-coding.q: The magnitude of Claude really hit me at Glitch Residency, where vibe coding was the air everyone breathed at the chateau; it was everywhere, on every laptop, on every lip, a part of every discussion.
vibe-coding.qt: Timeline · 2025 · Art of the Year: Claude Opus 4.5

video.d: Moving images recorded and played back as electronic signals rather than on film. Portable equipment such as the Sony Portapak (1967) opened it to artists and started video art.

voyager.d: NASA's Voyager 1 and 2 probes, launched in 1977 and now in interstellar space. Each carries the Golden Record, a selection of sounds and images from Earth curated by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan.

weaving.d: Making cloth by interlacing threads on a loom. The punched cards of the Jacquard loom link weaving to the history of computing, and many artists treat it as code.

web-2-0.d: The web of the 2000s, built around platforms where users post and share their own content: blogs, YouTube, Facebook and Twitter.
web-2-0.q: Ed Fornieles: We came up within the moment of Web 2.0, where suddenly there was a new paradigm to make sense of.
web-2-0.qt: Ed Fornieles on Art as Human Sacrifice

windows.d: Microsoft's operating system with a graphical interface, first released in 1985. It runs most of the world's personal computers.

world-wide-web.d: The system of linked pages reached over the Internet, proposed by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989 and opened to the public in 1991. It gave rise to net art.
world-wide-web.q: One of the key moments in mass-media art but also in human history, Berners-Lee’s invention revolutionized the digital landscape as the visionary computer scientist conceived of the concept of the World Wide Web (WWW).
world-wide-web.qt: Timeline · 1989 · Tim Berners-Lee Invents the World Wide Web

3d-modeling.d: Building three-dimensional objects in software as meshes of points and surfaces. The models can be rendered, animated or printed.

3d-printing.d: Building physical objects layer by layer from a digital model.

actionscript.d: The programming language of Flash, used for interactive web art and games in the 2000s.

agentic-systems.d: AI systems that plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, using tools and acting on a person's behalf.

ai-models.d: Trained machine-learning systems that turn inputs into outputs: a prompt into an image, or a question into an answer. Examples range from image classifiers to large language models.

alphago.d: DeepMind's Go-playing program, which beat world champion Lee Sedol in 2016. Its unexpected 'move 37' became a touchstone for machine creativity.

amiga-1000.d: The first Commodore Amiga, launched in 1985 with advanced color graphics and sound. Andy Warhol made digital images on it at its launch.
amiga-1000.q: I discovered immediately that the Amiga 1000 was rare and unique in that it had immense possibilities for colors.

apple-ii.d: Apple's home computer of 1977, one of the first mass-produced personal computers with color graphics. Many artists and game makers started on it.
apple-ii.q: The Apple II (1977), Commodore 64 (1982) and Commodore Amiga (1985) all represent enough of a change, moving out of the research labs and into artist studios, that it's a whole other era.
apple-ii.qt: Casey Reas on the History of Generative Art - Part 2

bally-arcade.d: A home video game console released by Bally in 1978, built around the Z80 chip. Zgrass was developed for it in Chicago.

base.d: An Ethereum layer-2 network launched by Coinbase in 2023. Its low fees made it a common place to mint and collect art.

binary.d: Counting with only two digits, 0 and 1. All digital data, from text to images, is stored in binary.

blender.d: A free, open-source 3D creation suite for modeling, animation and rendering, created by Ton Roosendaal and made open source in 2002.

bots.d: Programs that act automatically online, posting, replying or trading. Twitter bots were a popular form of generative art and poetry in the 2010s.

boltzmann-machines.d: Neural networks that learn the probability of patterns in their data, introduced by Geoffrey Hinton and Terry Sejnowski in the mid-1980s. They were early generative models.

camera-tracking.d: Following a camera's position and movement so that live or computer-generated imagery can be matched to it.

cepstrum.d: In signal processing, the spectrum of the logarithm of a sound's spectrum, introduced in 1963. It separates a voice's pitch from its timbre and underlies speech recognition.
cepstrum.q: It’s called the Cepstrum and I implemented it that summer.
cepstrum.qt: A. Michael Noll on When It All Started

claude-code.d: Anthropic's coding agent, released in 2025, which works in a programmer's terminal to read, write and run code with Claude.

color-copier.d: An office machine that photocopies in color, first sold by Xerox in 1973. Sonia Landy Sheridan and her Generative Systems program in Chicago used it as an art medium.

computer-art.d: Art made with computers, a name first used for the work of the 1960s pioneers such as Georg Nees, Frieder Nake, A. Michael Noll and Vera Molnár. The first exhibitions were held in 1965.
computer-art.q: The reaction from the general public and from the artistic community upon seeing the first computer art was negative and bordered on hostile.
computer-art.qt: Timeline · 1965 · The World’s First Computer Art Exhibition: “Georg Nees: Computergrafik”, Studiengalerie der TH Stuttgart

deep-fakes.d: Realistic fake video, audio or images of real people made with AI. The term dates from 2017.

digital-art-scene.d: The artists, collectors, platforms and venues of digital art.

drawing-machine.d: A mechanical or computer-driven device that makes drawings, from 19th-century harmonographs to plotters and robot arms. Artists build them to share authorship with the machine.
drawing-machine.q: By 1971 Harold Cohen had built a computer-controlled drawing machine, which he showed at the Fall Joint Computer Conference.
drawing-machine.qt: Timeline · 1970 · Trained Artists Intervene with Computers

emulators.d: Software that imitates other hardware, letting old computers and game consoles run on new machines. They are important for preserving digital art.

erc-721.d: The Ethereum standard for non-fungible tokens, published in 2018, which defines how each token is unique and transferable. Most NFT art on Ethereum follows it.

facetime.d: Apple's video calling app, launched in 2010.

flame.d: Two things go by this name: the fractal flame algorithm, created by Scott Draves in 1992, which renders glowing, smoky forms and powers Electric Sheep; and Flame, high-end visual-effects software now made by Autodesk.

generative-photography.d: Photography made by systematic, rule-based procedures. Gottfried Jäger introduced the term at a 1968 exhibition in Bielefeld, following Max Bense's generative aesthetics.
generative-photography.q: Rather than thinking about photography as a mirror of the real world, Jäger’s generative photography was non-representational.

generative-grammar.d: Noam Chomsky's theory, set out in 1957, that a finite set of rules can generate every sentence of a language. Early computer poetry and generative art drew on it.

hash.d: A fixed-length string of characters computed from data by a hash function. In on-chain generative art, the hash of each mint transaction seeds the algorithm, so every output is unique.

holography.d: Recording light so as to reproduce a three-dimensional image, invented by Dennis Gabor in 1947 and practical once lasers arrived in the 1960s.

humanoid-robots.d: Robots built in the shape of the human body.

ibm-7090.d: A transistorized IBM mainframe introduced in 1959. A. Michael Noll made some of the first computer art on one at Bell Labs in the early 1960s.

ibm-pc.d: IBM's personal computer of 1981, whose open design became the standard for most PCs since.

kinetic-sculpture.d: Sculpture with moving parts, driven by motors, wind or the viewer. Calder's mobiles and Tinguely's machines are classic examples.
kinetic-sculpture.q: Kinetic sculpture was a critical predecessor to the digital motion of electronic (generative) art.
kinetic-sculpture.qt: Timeline · c. 1953 · “Antennae with Red and Blue Dots” by Alexander Calder

logo.d: An educational programming language created in 1967 by Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert and Cynthia Solomon. Its 'turtle' drew lines on screen as children gave it commands.
logo.q: I think Logo was an early seed of, “Yeah, we're learning procedural thinking, we're learning logic, but we're also making visual art at the same time.”
logo.qt: Casey Reas on the History of Generative Art - Part 1

long-form-generative-art.d: A format in which collectors mint outputs of a generative algorithm one at a time, each seed producing a unique work, until an edition of hundreds or thousands is complete. Art Blocks established it in 2020.

macintosh.d: Apple's personal computer, launched in January 1984 with a graphical interface and a mouse. Programs like MacPaint made it an early tool for digital artists and designers.

markov-chain.d: A model in which each next step depends only on the current one, set out by Andrey Markov in 1906. Early text and music generators used Markov chains.

minecraft.d: A sandbox video game, first released in 2009, in which players build worlds out of blocks. It is the best-selling video game of all time.

mnist.d: A dataset of 70,000 handwritten digits, released in 1998 and long the standard first test for machine-learning models.
mnist.q: The first thing that I trained was taking little images of handwritten digits from a data set called MNIST that's really overused in machine learning research but it's also very fast to train on.

modem.d: A device that sends digital data over telephone lines by converting it to sound and back. It connected early home computers to bulletin boards and the internet.

moviola.d: A machine for viewing and editing film, introduced in 1924, standard in film editing for decades.

oil-painting.d: Painting with pigments bound in drying oil, the dominant medium of European painting since the 15th century. Some generative artists use robots or plotters to paint in oil.

on-chain-storage.d: Keeping an artwork's data inside the blockchain itself rather than on an outside server, so the work survives as long as the chain does.

oscillographs.d: Electronic images made by recording signals on an oscilloscope screen, often with a camera. Ben Laposky and Herbert W. Franke made some of the first electronic art this way in the 1950s.

oskar.d: A programming language for animation that Larry Cuba is developing, named after the abstract filmmaker Oskar Fischinger. It builds on RAP, the language Cuba used for his earlier films.

photogrammetry.d: Measuring and rebuilding 3D objects or spaces from many overlapping photographs.

pioneer.d: NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 probes, launched in 1972 and 1973 and the first to cross the asteroid belt. Each carries the Pioneer plaque, an engraved message to anyone who might find it.

polaroids.d: Instant photographs that develop within minutes of being taken, from the cameras of Edwin Land's Polaroid company, first sold in 1948.

printers.d: Machines that put computer output onto paper. Early computer artists used line printers and plotters to make their first images.

programming.d: Writing instructions in a language a computer can carry out. For code-based artists, the program is the work's medium and often the work itself.
programming.q: However, what is unique is that programming is like the brush with the whole watercolor box.

projection.d: Casting an image onto a surface with a projector. Projection mapping fits moving images to buildings, objects and rooms.

prompting.d: Writing instructions or descriptions, called prompts, to steer a generative AI model. Choosing the words has become a craft of its own.

prompts.d: The text instructions or descriptions given to a generative AI model to steer what it produces.

rust.d: A programming language focused on speed and safety, started at Mozilla, with version 1.0 released in 2015.

seedream-4-0.d: ByteDance's image generation and editing model, released in 2025.

sensors.d: Devices that measure the physical world, such as movement, light, sound or heat, and turn it into data. They let artworks respond to viewers and their surroundings.

smartphones.d: Pocket computers with touchscreens, cameras and constant internet access, mainstream since the iPhone of 2007. They changed how art is made, seen and shared.

sprites.d: Small 2D images, such as characters or objects, moved around the screen in video games and computer graphics.

stereograms.d: Images that create an illusion of depth, either as image pairs viewed one per eye or as single-image 'Magic Eye' patterns.

terminal.d: A text-only interface for typing commands to a computer, once a device of its own and now a window on screen.
terminal.q: The terminal is fast and something I'm really familiar with.

three-js.d: A JavaScript library for 3D graphics in the web browser, started by Ricardo Cabello (mrdoob) in 2010. Many on-chain generative artworks use it.

touchdesigner.d: A node-based visual programming environment from the Toronto company Derivative for real-time graphics and interaction. It is widely used for live visuals and installations.
touchdesigner.q: Although TouchDesigner is where I feel closest to God because I can make software that controls things in the real world in real time.
touchdesigner.qt: Wendi Yan & Karyn Nakamura on the Artifice of Knowledge

unix.d: An operating system created at Bell Labs in 1969 by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie. Its ideas underlie Linux and macOS.

video-installation.d: Artwork that places video in a physical space, often with several screens or projections arranged for the viewer to move through. Nam June Paik was a pioneer.

voice-cloning.d: Making an AI copy of a real person's voice from recordings of their speech.

vr-headset.d: A head-mounted display with screens for each eye and motion tracking, used to view virtual reality.

world-models.d: AI systems that learn how an environment behaves so they can predict and generate what happens next, in some cases whole explorable worlds.
